topic: Google Agent Quality Flywheel Skill Guide 2026: Testing and Grading Agents From Your Coding Agent

competitors.title: Why evaluate agents - Agent Development Kit (ADK)
key_points: ADK positions agent evaluation as different from deterministic unit tests because LLM agents vary across runs.
The core evaluation split is trajectory/tool-use quality plus final-response quality.
ADK supports test files for unit-test-like checks, evalsets for longer multi-turn integration tests, Web UI evaluation, pytest, CLI evaluation, and conformance testing.

Built-in criteria include tool trajectory score, response match, semantic final response match, rubric-based response quality, rubric-based tool-use quality, hallucination, safety, multi-turn task success, multi-turn trajectory quality, and multi-turn tool-use quality.
Default criteria are strict on trajectory by default: tool_trajectory_avg_score at 1.0 and response_match_score at 0.8.
Trace view is a strong differentiator: developers can inspect events, requests, responses, and graph/tool-call flow when an eval fails.

competitors.title: How good is your AI? Gen AI evaluation at every stage, explained
key_points: Google Cloud frames evaluation as a continuous lifecycle from prompt/model selection through production agent monitoring.
Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation Service supports batch evaluation, pointwise/pairwise evaluation, rubric customization, autorater evaluation, and production-oriented agent evaluation.
For agents, Google stresses that final-answer grading is insufficient; teams must also evaluate tool choice, action sequence, memory use, and trajectory.
Results integrate with Vertex AI Experiments so runs can be compared across prompt, model, and agent versions.
Google explicitly identifies open problems: cold-start eval data, multi-agent evaluation, and real-world agent simulation.

competitors.title: AI Agent Evaluation Metrics - DeepEval
key_points: DeepEval organizes agent evaluation into three layers: reasoning, action, and execution.
Reasoning metrics include plan quality and plan adherence; action metrics include tool correctness and argument correctness; execution metrics include task completion and step efficiency.
The article highlights common failure modes: right tool with wrong arguments, good plan not followed, task completed with redundant costly steps.
DeepEval argues trace-level evaluation is necessary because agent failures are hidden inside intermediate reasoning and tool calls.
A practical insight for the article: do not treat task completion alone as quality; measure efficiency and argument correctness separately.

competitors.title: Agent Evaluation Readiness Checklist - LangChain
key_points: LangChain recommends manually reviewing 20 to 50 real traces before building evaluation infrastructure.
The checklist separates capability evals from regression evals because they answer different questions: what can the agent do versus does it still work.
It recommends starting with full-trace evaluation, then adding single-step and multi-turn checks as needed.
Dataset quality is emphasized over volume: hand-reviewed examples are more valuable than large unverified synthetic sets.
Grader design should default to code-based checks for objective properties, LLM-as-judge for subjective quality, and human review for calibration and ambiguous cases.
A strong editorial angle is the trace-to-dataset flywheel: production failures become future regression tests.

competitors.title: Agent observability: The complete guide for 2026 - Braintrust
key_points: Braintrust frames observability as the substrate for evaluation: capture tool calls, reasoning chains, state transitions, memory reads/writes, and model responses.
The minimum viable trace schema includes span type, inputs, outputs, timing, errors/retries, and identifiers.
For multi-agent systems, Braintrust stresses parent-child span propagation across handoffs so downstream failures can be traced to upstream context mistakes.
The article connects online evaluation on production traces with offline golden-case evaluation and CI gates.
A concrete flywheel model: score live traces, convert failures into eval cases, run the same checks locally/in CI/production, and block releases when quality regresses.

competitors.title: Best AI Evaluation Tools for Agents in 2026: Agent-First vs LLM-Only Platforms
key_points: Latitude's comparison argues that agent-first tools must model complete execution trajectories, not isolated prompt-response pairs.
It compares Braintrust, LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Galileo, Maxim, and Latitude across multi-turn support, state management, tool use, issue discovery, and auto-generated evals.
The article's useful contrast: LLM-first tools can show that a final step failed, while agent-native traces can identify the earlier tool argument or handoff that caused it.
This is a competitor-style piece that helps position the target article around agent-native quality loops rather than generic LLM evaluation.

stats.fact: ADK's default evaluation criteria require a 1.0 tool trajectory average score and a 0.8 response match score when no custom criteria are supplied.

ADK lists 11 built-in agent evaluation criteria spanning tool trajectories, semantic final response matching, rubric quality, hallucination, safety, user simulation quality, and multi-turn success/tool-use quality.
Google Cloud's June 13, 2025 Gen AI Evaluation update added batch evaluation, autorater customization, rubrics-driven evaluation, and agent evaluation capabilities around trajectory and tool use.
LangChain's March 27, 2026 checklist recommends manually reviewing 20 to 50 real agent traces before building automated eval infrastructure.
LangChain recommends starting LLM-as-judge calibration with at least 20 labeled examples and growing toward roughly 100 examples for production-grade confidence.
DeepEval's agent metric taxonomy covers three evaluation layers: reasoning, action/tool use, and execution/task completion.
Braintrust's 2026 guide says a production-ready trace should capture tool calls, reasoning steps, state transitions, and memory operations.

angles: Define the 'quality flywheel' as a loop: capture traces, label failures, convert them into ADK evalsets, run local/CI evals, deploy, monitor production traces, then feed new failures back into the suite.
Make the coding-agent-specific twist explicit: the agent should create its own eval cases while it works, not wait for a separate QA team.
Position Google ADK as the inner-loop tool for fast local debugging, and Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation as the outer-loop system for scale, autorater calibration, and experiment tracking.
Separate 'agent said done' from 'work is actually done' by checking state changes: tests pass, files changed as expected, PR created, issue status updated, or API side effect occurred.
Warn against brittle exact-path grading: use exact trajectory only for strict workflows; use rubric/tool-quality metrics when multiple valid paths exist.
Use a tiered metric panel: final answer, tool trajectory, argument correctness, state change verification, cost/latency, hallucination/safety, and multi-turn memory retention.
Use the 'skill' framing: a reusable coding-agent skill can include eval templates, trace-review checklists, failure taxonomy, and CI gate commands.
